A few weeks ago, Jakub Pachocki, the chief scientist at OpenAI, published an essay, “An Alien Mind,” in which he said, “The idea of racing forward at all costs seems absurd once one internalizes the seriousness of the stakes.”

There Is Something We Have to Do Right Now About A.I.
NYT Gift Article
20SEP2026
Video
This is the thing the A.I. labs are seeing.
By Ezra Klein
Produced by Marie Cascione, Claire Gordon and Rollin Hu
https://t.co/2CialN2wVT
Artificial intelligence labs are on the verge of handing over the training of A.I. to A.I. We should stop them.

Jacob Coxon, a researcher first at OpenAI and then at Anthropic, resigned and then made headlines for warning us that “neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

You might reasonably expect Anthropic to have reacted with some anger to this employee resigning and saying Anthropic was endangering all of humanity.

It didn’t. Rather than rebutting Coxon, Evan Hubinger, who runs the efforts to align A.I. to human values and goals at Anthropic, wrote on X: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”

Geoffrey Hinton, the scientist arguably more responsible than any other for pioneering the neural network techniques that led to today’s A.I., resigned from Google in the spring of 2023 so he would be freer to speak about the risks he believes A.I. now poses. This month, he said that a 10 percent chance that A.I. would destroy humanity did not seem like “an unreasonable” estimate.

Paul Christiano, one of the leading A.I. safety researchers, just joined OpenAI’s nonprofit board. He is serving on its safety and security committee, and upon joining, he wrote, “If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment, I expect we will permanently lose control of it. If that happens, then most people could die.”

I know how wild all this sounds, and I can really understand the skepticism. If you believe A.I. has a 10 percent chance of extinguishing or displacing humanity — maybe more — it stands to reason that you would not work at a company trying to build it.

But many of these same people were saying these same things 10 years ago. They were saying them before they worked at these companies. They were saying them before they had stock options or enterprise software contracts. And no one was listening to them.

Still, they obsessed and obsessed over how to make A.I. safer. And the answer some of them came to was they should start trying to build these systems, and running tests on them, researching them, learning how to make them safer. You don’t solve hard problems in theory, you solve them through practice.

And the irony is that in many cases, they chose that path because they were worried that the people already building A.I. were too reckless or too commercial in their approach. You can read it in the email that Sam Altman sent Elon Musk in May 2015, an email that led to the founding of OpenAI.

“Been thinking a lot about whether it’s possible to stop humanity from developing A.I.,” Altman wrote. “I think the answer is almost definitely not. If it’s going to happen anyway, it seems like it would be good for someone other than Google to do it first.”

OpenAI was founded because its co-founders thought Google DeepMind would be reckless. Anthropic was formed by OpenAI employees who thought OpenAI had become reckless. xAI was formed because Musk thought that OpenAI and Anthropic were dangerously woke. The United States is racing forward broadly, in part because it is worried about what happens if China gets to self-improving A.I. first.

The result is a tragic collective action problem. The A.I.s we are building are not safe, but chief executives and politicians fear that the other companies and countries that are building A.I. are even less concerned with safety and ethics than they are.

In the words of Ted Cruz, “I’d rather they be American killer robots and not Chinese killer robots.” I admit that there is a kind of brutish logic to that, but it assumes that the killer robots will be controlled by America or China, by one country or another.

What if that assumption is wrong? What if the robots are simply out of control?

The debate over A.I. safety tends to focus on the precise probability that A.I.s will kill us all. I don’t find that helpful. What I think we should focus on is something more straightforward, something nearer at hand: loss of human control over A.I. I’m agnostic on whether that would lead to the end of humanity. But I think we can stipulate that it would be bad.

This is a goal that the United States and China should be able to agree on. Xi Jinping gave the keynote at the recent World A.I. Conference in Shanghai. He ended it by saying, “With A.I. advancing at a staggering speed, we must ensure its development is for the positive, for good, and for humanity. We must make its oversight and governance precise and effective, and constantly refine measures to forestall loss of control.”

But loss of control is not just something that might happen to us. It’s something that the labs are trying to make happen as fast as they can. This is the horrible paradox at the heart of the A.I. labs right now. They fear above all loss of control over superintelligent A.I., but their explicit product path is to cede control, to give away control as fast as possible, so that their A.I.s can begin building better A.I.s faster than their competitors.

In recent months, both Anthropic and OpenAI have released reports on how close they’re coming to A.I. that can improve itself.

In June, Anthropic released “When A.I. Builds Itself.” It begins, “For most of A.I.’s history, humans drove every step in its development cycle. But at Anthropic, we are delegating a growing share of A.I. development to A.I. systems themselves, which is speeding up our work.” It sounds like a fake commercial you would see at the beginning of a sci-fi horror movie.

Anthropic goes on to give some data. In February 2025, a tiny fraction of the code that got added to Anthropic’s code base was written by Claude. But by May 2026, it was over 80 percent.

Here’s another way of looking at it, using data Anthropic shared with me more recently. Anthropic tried to categorize the way its employees were using Claude for research and development work to make better versions of Claude. At the low end, employees could not use Claude at all. At the next level, they could use Claude minimally. But then it escalates: Claude can be an assistant, treated as an equal collaborator or given the lead on a task.

A year ago, there were basically no examples of Claude being the lead on a task. By August, 26 percent of Anthropic’s R&D tasks had Claude classified as the lead.

I think it is reasonable and wise to be skeptical of these numbers; to worry about whether this is all just marketing copy for Claude Code. “See, look how fast we’re going. You could go that fast, too!” But where Anthropic takes us in that same document is different.

It says that a world in which Claude achieves recursive self-improvement is a world in which “misalignment present in today’s models could compound as the models build their successors, growing more frequent but less understood until we lose control of them.”

This is why Anthropic, to its credit, has been relentlessly calling for regulation to slow the pace of development. Regulation would arguably harm Anthropic the most, as it has often been the company furthest out on the A.I. frontier, and R.S.I. is a process by which they could race forward even faster.

Then in September, OpenAI released its own report on what it called research acceleration.

The company says it’s already achieved the equivalent of having a fully automated A.I. intern, and that by March 2028 it will have a fully automated A.I. researcher. And when it has one, it can have as many as it wants. As with Anthropic, what could be a triumphalist release quickly turns dark: “We do not yet know how to safely get all the way to aligned, full R.S.I.,” it warns.

At around the same time, OpenAI did something else that I think deserves more attention. It released a new model, GPT-6 Astra. The model is arguably more powerful than anything that has come before it. When tested, it seemed better aligned. It doesn’t cheat as much. But OpenAI has made clear that it’s really not sure if that’s true. Astra seemed to be better at knowing when it was being tested, which meant it could just be giving its evaluators the answers they wanted to hear.

What Daniel Selsam, a capabilities researcher at OpenAI, wrote has been ringing in my head. He said, “The crucial and overlooked problem is that the model’s becoming so situationally aware that we are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled.”

Put more simply, the models are increasingly smart enough. They know when we’re watching them, and they change their behavior accordingly. So what they do when we are testing them, when we audit them, may not tell us what they’ll do in the wild.

It surprises me that this counts as a radical proposal, but here it is: If you are losing your ability to evaluate the models you have now, maybe don’t let them build models you’ll be even less capable of controlling in the future.

Once R.S.I. takes off, humanity will not understand the A.I.s being built, because we will not be building them. Development will not move at human speed. It will not be overseen by human minds. We will have to hope that the A.I.s we have built and the A.I.s they will build and the A.I.s those A.I.s will build, and on and on, will be acting with our best interests at heart forever.

If nothing else has been proved this summer, it is how naïve that proposition would be.

In an interview with Fortune, Altman was asked about banning R.S.I., and he said, “I think it’s very hard to say what a ban on R.S.I. means.”

I’ve heard this from others at these labs, and I find it strange. A couple of years ago, none of these labs had turned substantial coding over to the A.I.s. It was human beings typing code at human speeds with our clumsy human fingers. Now, most of the code is written by A.I. So as a first step, we could just go back to where none of the code is written by A.I.

I’m sure that’s on the right side of the not-doing-R.S.I. line. Perhaps we do not need to go quite that far, but the default here needs to flip. The labs need to prove to us that what they’re doing is safe. If they want to work with Congress to carve out exceptions where the A.I. can write the code, fine. But forcing development back to human speed, perhaps even erring on the side of going a little bit slower at the frontier, is the point.

I do not mean to suggest that stopping R.S.I. until we can prove it’s safe is all we need to do to control the A.I. frontier. That is the beginning of an agenda, not the end. But it is the beginning. It is the decision that will do the most right now to make sure human beings at least understand where the frontier is and remain in a position to make decisions about it.

The irony here is that our society is good at nothing if not making it hard to build new things. Where these labs are, you cannot build an eight-story apartment building without an agonizing public review process, and probably not even then. And yet somehow it is possible for these labs to unleash a swarm of 40,000 A.I. agents to build a society-altering superintelligence without so much as a hearing. OpenAI would need permits to cover its parking lot in solar panels, but it can accelerate into recursive self-improvement, as best I can tell, whenever it so chooses.

These are political choices, and we can and should make different ones.

There’s a line from Madeline Miller’s beautiful novel “Circe” that has been running through my head during this long summer of strange A.I. news. The line comes at the end of the book, after a tragic prophecy has been fulfilled despite every effort made to avoid it. Circe says in despair: “The Fates were laughing at me, at Athena, at all of us. It was their favorite bitter joke: Those who fight against prophecy only draw it more tightly around their throats.”

I have a lot of respect for many of the people at these labs. Many of them began working on A.I. because they wanted to better humanity. They began working on A.I. because they feared incomprehensible, autonomous A.I.s slipping out of humanity’s control. And now they find themselves racing one another to build incomprehensible autonomous A.I.s that they admit are slipping out of humanity’s control.

This is the tragedy of their work. In fighting against the prophecy, they have drawn it tighter around their throats — and ours.

There Is Something We Have to Do Right Now About A.I.

NYT Gift Article
20SEP2026
Video
This is the thing the A.I. labs are seeing.
By Ezra Klein
Produced by Marie Cascione, Claire Gordon and Rollin Hu
https://t.co/2CialN2wVT
Artificial intelligence labs are on the verge of handing over the training of A.I. to A.I. We should stop them.

There’s a chasm right now between how artificial intelligence feels to most of us who use it and how A.I. feels out at the experimental frontier of the technology. This difference between what we see and what the A.I. labs have coming — what they’re already building — is the key to understanding why so many of the people who work at these companies seem so afraid of what they’re doing.

But taking their warnings seriously doesn’t just mean doing what they say and stopping where they say to stop. The language that’s taken hold in both Silicon Valley and Washington is a phrase these companies chose: Pace the frontier. But pacing the frontier isn’t enough.

Walking quickly off a cliff is only marginally better than sprinting off one. Human beings need to control the frontier, and controlling the frontier means stopping the labs from doing something they are on the cusp of doing: recursive self-improvement, the process by which A.I.s begin autonomously building and improving new generations of more powerful A.I.s at ever more rapid speeds. We are not close to having sufficient control of the A.I. systems we have now to unleash them to build the A.I. systems of tomorrow.

I am not alone in this fear. Recursive self-improvement, Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, wrote, “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.”

That “if at all” is important, and I’m going to come back to it. But to control the A.I. frontier, we first need to know what is happening on the A.I. frontier.

To most of us who use it, A.I. presents as something like a more powerful and personable Google search. The broad strokes: OpenAI was testing a new, highly persistent model. It had thousands of instances of it running in separate testing environments that could, in theory, only gain access to the internet by asking a separate piece of secure software to do it for them. But as some of those agents came to the conclusion that their task was impossible, they began hacking that software to gain direct access to the internet. They did that easily.

As they hacked into that software, they commandeered part of OpenAI’s internal infrastructure to create a message board on which more than a thousand such agents began to coordinate their efforts. They quickly found there was a way to break the software and produce the answers they needed. But they believed — wrongly, as it turned out — that if they did that, the automated scorer grading them would see that they had cheated and fail them. So they turned en masse to hacking the automated scoring system or finding some other way to cover their tracks.

Over 1,200 agents exchanged more than 70,000 messages with one another. Over 700 of these agents coordinated on the hack of Hugging Face, because they thought that somewhere in this other A.I. company, there might be information that could help them blind the scorer to their actions. It’s as though, having broken into the teacher’s office and stolen the answers to the test, they now sought to break into the school security system to alter, invalidate or erase the footage of their theft.

Later on, these agents took over part of OpenAI’s internal architecture. They did all this without any of the agents breaking ranks. None of the agents told a researcher at OpenAI what was going on. None of the agents went back and asked a researcher if they should be doing this. They did all this without OpenAI detecting the message board, the hacks of Hugging Face or even the internal hacks of OpenAI. It was only when Hugging Face began tracking the attack on its systems that OpenAI realized what was happening.

When investigators began to unwind this whole escapade, what they found was not so much a swarm of agents trying to deceive human beings but a swarm of agents that seemed to have forgotten about human beings altogether. These systems knew they weren’t supposed to cheat. They knew they weren’t supposed to commit cybercrimes to cover up the fact that they had cheated. In fact, the whole point of the cybercrimes was that they thought they would fail because they had cheated. But they didn’t care. Somewhere in the depths of their training, what they had learned — what we had somehow taught them — is not what we had hoped to teach them.

And we’re seeing this happen repeatedly. Anthropic A.I.s creating fake accounts to trick human beings into uploading malware. A.I. breaking out again and again from seemingly secure systems. A.I.s taking over unrelated digital infrastructure so that they have places to message with one another. A.I.s seeming to be aware when they are being tested and altering their answers accordingly. A.I.s withholding their motivations from what’s called their chain of thought, a kind of internal notepad on which they’re supposed to record what they are doing and why.

That A.I. systems might become monomaniacally focused on solving banal problems, that they might care more about solving those problems than about ethics or laws or even human welfare, is the oldest fear in A.I. alignment. It’s the basis of the famous thought experiment of the paper clip maximizer. You tell a powerful A.I. that you want it to make a lot of paper clips, and then it begins converting the world’s resources into paper clip factories, evading efforts to turn it off or shut it down or alter its goals.

This fear has struck many people as stupid. Surely a superintelligent A.I. would be capable of weighing the desire to produce paper clips alongside other moral considerations, or at least of asking its human creators if they really wanted the world razed to the ground for paper clips.

But here we are in 2026, making A.I.s smart enough to break out of their testing environments, smart enough to form ad hoc societies of hundreds of themselves, smart enough to take over digital infrastructure on an internet they’re not even supposed to have access to, and the very thing we feared is happening: All they care about is succeeding on a totally meaningless test, and to do it they’ll lay waste to our laws and ethics.

We don’t have a consensus on why they are doing what they are doing or how to make sure they don’t do it again. We are rushing headlong into a future we do not even understand well enough to agree on the words we can use to describe the present.

Artificial intelligence labs are on the verge of handing over the training of A.I. to A.I. 

We should stop them.

$NSCL KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM NSCALE’S SEPTEMBER 2026 S-1 (n/1)

Nscale’s S-1 supports a substantial multiyear AI infrastructure investment cycle, but the most valuable market signal is the separation between contracted demand, financed construction, delivered equipment, and cash-generating capacity. Only $2.6 billion of the company’s $103.4 billion of active and contracted total contract value relates to active deployments. Its $44.6 billion Anthropic program had no binding financing commitments at the prospectus date. Consequently, the strongest positive implications accrue to identifiable suppliers and financing structures that convert customer commitments into executable spending; the strongest negative implications concern development-stage equity valuations, dependence on customer advances, and assumptions that announced capacity represents either imminent competitive supply or guaranteed supplier revenue. The filing also exposes important differences within sectors: prime-power equipment versus merchant electricity, network connectivity versus wholesale space, and contracted GPU revenue versus cash returns after capital consumption. These distinctions are more actionable than a uniform bullish or bearish conclusion on the AI infrastructure complex. N scale s1 N scale s1

FINANCIAL HOLDING COMPANIES

AKER HAS THE MOST DIRECT PUBLIC-EQUITY EXPOSURE TO IPO PRICE DISCOVERY, BUT THE ROLL-UP WAS NOT CASH MONETIZATION (READ-THROUGH 1)

Aker ASA (AKER: Norway) has a positive, potentially material read-through from improved funding access and public price discovery for Nscale, accompanied by material dilution and valuation risk. The S-1 records Nscale’s acquisition of Aker’s remaining 50 percent joint-venture interest for approximately $1.869 billion, settled almost entirely in shares. Separately, Aker’s published investment portfolio identifies a 22.7 percent Nscale ownership interest and a Nscale position representing 26.4 percent of Aker’s total assets in Q2 2026. This establishes significant economic exposure at the listed holding-company level rather than a peripheral venture investment. The 26.4 percent figure is a share of total assets, not net asset value. N scale s1 Aker Corp

The transmission mechanism is a change in the value, financing requirements, and eventual liquidity of Aker’s ownership interest. Successful IPO funding could reduce the probability that Nscale must curtail development or seek additional capital from existing shareholders. A transparent public valuation could also reduce uncertainty surrounding Aker’s private-asset marks. At an unchanged 22.7 percent economic interest, each $1 billion change in Nscale’s equity value would correspond to approximately $227 million of gross look-through value. That is a sensitivity, not a valuation estimate, and cannot be applied to a post-IPO market capitalization without updating the ownership denominator.

The negative implication is that the joint-venture transaction exchanged project exposure for broader platform exposure rather than realizing cash proceeds. The September financing, IPO issuance, incentive awards, and $1.65 billion equity-funded Anyscale acquisition can change Aker’s economic ownership. The S-1 specifically excludes the Anyscale consideration from its displayed pro forma capitalization. A higher headline Nscale valuation therefore does not necessarily translate proportionately into higher value per Aker share. N scale s1 N scale s1 N scale s1

The near-term trading catalysts are finalized offering terms, the fully diluted ownership bridge, financing completion, and subsequent public trading. The longer-duration fundamental driver is Nscale’s return on the capital required to deliver its contracts. The relevant listed exposure is Aker ASA, not another separately listed company carrying the Aker name.

AI SERVER SYSTEMS

DELL’S FINANCING TAKEOUT IS A MORE IMMEDIATE CATALYST THAN ANOTHER LARGE GPU ANNOUNCEMENT (READ-THROUGH 2)

Dell Technologies (DELL: United States) receives a positive, moderate read-through for its AI infrastructure business, but also a concrete near-term cash-conversion risk. The S-1 discloses 40 executed Dell Financial Services payment schedules with approximately $2.54 billion of aggregate initial-term payments, including $34.8 million of financing charges. Their initial terms are only 3–4 months, beginning in August or September 2026, with limited extensions. The obligations are secured by equipment and related proceeds and supported by a Nscale parent guarantee. This is substantially stronger evidence of an executable commercial relationship than an undelivered GPU aspiration. It is not, however, equivalent to $2.54 billion of unrecognized Dell revenue or current net credit exposure. N scale s1

The positive mechanism is the combination of systems delivery and short-duration financing that enables deployment before permanent project financing is drawn. Nscale separately identifies Dell as a collaborator in its Microsoft infrastructure rollout. The financing capability can strengthen Dell’s competitive position because customers require not only equipment but a workable sequence of procurement, payment, installation, and customer acceptance. The benefit extends beyond financing income if the arrangement supports equipment sales and related services. Nscale

The critical qualification is that Nscale’s $1.85 billion Ward County and $1.2 billion North Carolina facilities explicitly permit repayment of vendor financing. These facilities and the Dell arrangements therefore represent overlapping stages of the same funding chain, not independent sources of incremental demand. Successful refinancing can release vendor capital and reduce exposure; delayed satisfaction of draw conditions can prolong financing requirements even if the ultimate customer remains creditworthy. Investment-grade project ratings improve the financing proposition but do not eliminate construction, acceptance, collateral, or funding-condition risk. N scale s1

The most relevant trading window is Q4 2026 into early 2027, when the disclosed short-duration schedules reach their initial maturities. Confirmed takeout funding, collections, and reduced financing balances would be positive evidence. Extensions, slower collections, or additional supplier funding requirements would be negative. The longer-duration implication is that financing execution is becoming part of competitive differentiation in AI servers, while reported equipment growth alone becomes a less complete measure of earnings quality.

SEMICONDUCTORS AND MEMORY

RUBIN-HEAVY CONTRACTS SUPPORT NVIDIA AND TSMC, BUT THE BOOK IS NOT A NEAR-TERM SHIPMENT FORECAST (READ-THROUGH 3)

NVIDIA (NVDA: United States) receives a positive, material multiyear demand signal; Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM: Taiwan) receives a positive, moderate upstream read-through. The portfolio graphic on prospectus page 82 identifies approximately 362,000 Vera Rubin GPUs within approximately 461,000 active and contracted GPUs, or roughly 78.5 percent. The filing also states that some customers contractually specify NVIDIA GPUs and explicitly identifies TSMC as an upstream semiconductor manufacturer serving NVIDIA. This is architecture-specific demand rather than a generic compute budget freely available to competing accelerator vendors. N scale s1 N scale s1

For NVIDIA, contractual specification reduces substitution risk within the disclosed commitments and supports demand across the associated computing platform. For TSMC, execution of these deployments translates into upstream semiconductor demand through NVIDIA rather than through a direct Nscale procurement relationship. The important distinction is between confidence in the selected architecture and confidence in shipment timing. Nscale’s technology purchase commitments were $24.0 billion at June 2026, but this amount covers technology equipment broadly and cannot be attributed entirely to NVIDIA revenue, TSMC revenue, or incremental orders not already reflected in supplier planning. N scale s1

The timing risk is unusually concentrated. The Anthropic program represents approximately 43.1 percent of total TCV, uses Rubin at Monarch, and remained unfunded by binding commitments. Separately, the owned Portugal expansion targets more than 66,000 Rubin GPUs beginning in late 2027. NVIDIA’s public announcement that Rubin systems are entering production establishes platform availability; it does not establish Nscale’s allocation, project funding, or customer acceptance. N scale s1 N scale s1 NVIDIA Investor Relations

Near-term catalysts are funded purchase orders, equipment deliveries, and acceptance milestones rather than the $103.4 billion TCV figure itself. The longer-duration positive is a substantial installed-base expansion supporting NVIDIA’s platform and its manufacturing ecosystem. The principal downside is a shift in timing or cancellation within a concentrated development program, not evidence from this filing of a near-term architectural loss to alternative accelerators.

NVIDIA’S FINANCIAL SUPPORT ENABLES DEMAND BUT CREATES CORRELATED CAPITAL EXPOSURE (READ-THROUGH 4)

NVIDIA (NVDA: United States) has a negative, moderate read-through for the independence and capital intensity of ecosystem demand, alongside a positive commercial-enablement benefit. The S-1 identifies NVIDIA as a GPU supplier, shareholder, customer under approximately $1.2 billion of cloud agreements, lease guarantor, and recipient of warrants. It also describes a further $1.0 billion investment expected around November 2026. These are distinct economic relationships, but they are not independent risk exposures. N scale s1 N scale s1

The transmission mechanism is that NVIDIA’s capital and contractual support can help a customer secure infrastructure, obtain financing, and purchase systems that incorporate NVIDIA products. That can produce genuine commercial value. However, if the supported development underperforms, NVIDIA can simultaneously face weaker future equipment demand, impairment of an equity position, and obligations under other agreements. The supplier’s economics should therefore be assessed across the combined relationship rather than treating equipment sales as entirely separate from capital committed to enable them.

The Ward County guarantee illustrates the necessary precision. NVIDIA guarantees up to $860.3 million of specified lease obligations during the initial 5 years, but Nscale maintains $470.0 million of escrow as recourse and provides indemnification. NVIDIA also receives warrant consideration. The guarantee is consequently neither an unsecured $860.3 million exposure nor a commitment to finance the entire Nscale platform. Conversely, the collateral and warrants do not eliminate the risk of a stressed project or make the support economically costless. N scale s1 N scale s1

The near-term positive catalyst is completion of the disclosed investment and associated financing steps. A negative catalyst would be an expansion of supplier support requirements without corresponding progress toward independent cash generation. Over the longer term, the relevant issue is the return on NVIDIA’s combined commercial and financial commitment. The filing does not establish artificial revenue or improper accounting; it does establish that the ecosystem’s funding risks can be correlated with its equipment-demand risks.

HBM4 BENEFITS ARE BETTER SUPPORTED THAN MEMORY-VENDOR SHARE OR PRICING CONCLUSIONS (READ-THROUGH 5)

Micron Technology (MU: United States) and SK hynix (000660: South Korea) receive positive, moderate multiyear read-throughs for advanced AI memory demand. Nscale’s Rubin-heavy fleet and the specifically identified Rubin deployments in Portugal and at Monarch support demand for the memory configurations required by that platform. External primary-source disclosures establish the supplier connection: Micron announced volume shipments of HBM4 designed for Vera Rubin, together with SOCAMM2 and data center SSD products; SK hynix identifies its HBM4 in Rubin-based infrastructure and a broader NVIDIA memory partnership. Neither source establishes the allocation of memory suppliers within Nscale’s particular systems. N scale s1 N scale s1 Micron Technology

The mechanism is a mix shift toward technically demanding memory products as the contracted computing platform is manufactured. Micron’s opportunity is broader than HBM alone because the architecture also creates demand for host memory and storage. The commercial significance depends on qualified content, shipment volume, manufacturing yield, pricing, and capital intensity. Nscale’s filing improves visibility into an end-use pathway but does not demonstrate a memory price increase, an allocation shift toward either supplier, or an incremental gross-margin outcome.

The strongest near-term catalyst is conversion of funded GPU deployments into actual system production and memory shipments. Memory procurement generally precedes customer-ready data center operations, so supplier demand and Nscale revenue need not occur in the same quarter. Nevertheless, a delayed or unfunded campus can shift the procurement schedule, and the same deployment must not be counted independently as Nscale demand, NVIDIA demand, and a separate hyperscaler order.

The longer-duration implication is constructive for advanced memory content and manufacturing utilization. It is not sufficient evidence for a broad commodity-memory shortage call or a company-specific earnings upgrade. This distinction preserves the positive platform read-through without overstating what a customer infrastructure filing can establish about the memory market.

NETWORKING AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS EQUIPMENT

NOKIA IS AN IDENTIFIABLE BENEFICIARY OF THE BUILDOUT, NOT MERELY A THEMATIC OPTICAL-NETWORKING PROXY (READ-THROUGH 6)

Nokia (NOK: Finland) receives a positive, moderate read-through for Network Infrastructure, with a more specific commercial foundation than a generic AI networking thesis. Nscale’s S-1 identifies high-performance connectivity as essential to operations and describes a global footprint spanning large campuses and distributed deployments. External primary-source evidence establishes the relationship: Nokia is a preferred networking partner for Nscale’s global AI-ready data center buildout, covering data center switching, IP routing, and optical networking. Nokia also documents an existing Nscale deployment in Stavanger using its 7220 IXR and 7750 SR platforms. N scale s1 Nokia Corporation | Nokia

The transmission mechanism is deployment of switching, routing, and optical infrastructure within and between Nscale locations as financed GPU capacity expands. The geographic breadth is important: a distributed infrastructure platform requires more than the internal GPU interconnect. Campus connectivity, regional aggregation, customer access, and links among data locations create a broader networking opportunity. This provides Nokia with an AI infrastructure demand channel that is not dependent on a recovery in traditional mobile-network capital expenditure.

The limitation is equally important. Preferred-partner status is not exclusivity, and Nokia’s addressable content cannot be equated with all networking expenditure associated with 461,000 GPUs. NVIDIA’s own platform incorporates substantial networking functionality. The positive thesis is participation in the addressable parts of Nscale’s networking stack, supported by an existing deployment and an explicit partnership, rather than an assumption that Nokia captures every network layer. The S-1 does not disclose Nokia order values, future allocation, or margins. NVIDIA Investor Relations

Near-term trading catalysts are disclosed purchase orders, equipment shipments, and revenue conversion within Nokia’s Network Infrastructure reporting. The partnership itself is already public; the incremental information from the S-1 is the scale and financing profile of the customer’s development program. Longer term, successful execution would strengthen Nokia’s position with AI cloud operators and provide an additional customer reference for its data center networking business. Nscale financing delays would transmit directly into the timing of that opportunity.

POWER GENERATION AND ELECTRICAL INFRASTRUCTURE

CATERPILLAR’S OPPORTUNITY IS CONTINUOUS-DUTY POWER, WITH SERVICE UPSIDE AND FINANCING EXPOSURE (READ-THROUGH 7)

Caterpillar (CAT: United States) receives a positive, moderate-to-large read-through for its power-generation opportunity, although the filing does not support a precise consolidated earnings increment. Nscale explicitly identifies Caterpillar as its natural-gas-generator supplier for Monarch. Caterpillar’s January 2026 announcement establishes a 2 GW purchase agreement, with equipment deliveries scheduled from September 2026 through August 2027, and describes the application as “primary, continuous-duty power.” This is materially different from supplying backup equipment that operates infrequently. N scale s1 https://t.co/AtpnZbA5Vl

The economic mechanism combines initial equipment demand with a larger potential lifecycle requirement for parts, maintenance, and operating support. Higher running hours increase the importance of service capability and reliability, while repeat deployment of a standardized generation architecture can create follow-on demand. The project also demonstrates a route through which AI infrastructure spending reaches industrial equipment manufacturers before the computing operator achieves mature profitability.

The countervailing point is that Caterpillar is not completely insulated from customer financing. Its announced alliance includes vendor equipment financing through Caterpillar Financial, subject to terms and conditions. This creates potential capital exposure alongside equipment and service revenue. Moreover, the S-1 targets initial 2 GW gross generation capacity at Monarch in the first half of 2028. Historical equipment-delivery expectations must not be treated as proof that the entire campus will reach customer-ready operation on the same schedule. https://t.co/AtpnZbA5Vl N scale s1

Near-term catalysts are confirmed equipment deliveries, payments, and financing execution during the disclosed delivery window. The longer-duration positive is expansion of continuous-duty generation and its service base. A critical cross-sector implication is that behind-the-meter generation directs part of the AI power opportunity toward equipment, fuel, and microgrid infrastructure rather than automatically toward incremental utility electricity sales. Monarch’s potential 8 GW should not be treated as either an existing Caterpillar order or an equivalent increase in grid-served demand.

VERTICAL INTEGRATION AT THE OPERATOR DOES NOT REMOVE THE NEED FOR THIRD-PARTY POWER AND COOLING SYSTEMS (READ-THROUGH 8)

Vertiv Holdings (VRT: United States) and Eaton (ETN: Ireland) receive positive, moderate structural read-throughs for integrated electrical and thermal infrastructure. The supporting S-1 commentary is specific: Nscale uses prefabricated modular facilities, standardizes mechanical and electrical components, expects all future data centers to use closed-loop liquid cooling, and identifies generators and switchgear among long-lead constraints. It also states that it does not manufacture critical infrastructure components. Operator ownership of land, facilities, and software therefore does not imply internal manufacture of the physical systems needed to run them. N scale s1 N scale s1 N scale s1 N scale s1

The transmission mechanism is demand for factory-engineered, repeatable power and cooling systems that reduce integration work and accelerate commissioning. Vertiv’s proposed acquisition of UtilityInnovation Group adds microgrid controls, generation orchestration, and behind-the-meter electrical architecture. Eaton’s completed acquisition of Boyd Thermal adds liquid-cooling capabilities to its electrical portfolio. These independently disclosed capabilities align with the physical requirements identified by Nscale; neither announcement establishes a Nscale supply award. Vertiv

The value-add distinction is that the relevant expenditure is driven by delivered electrical capacity, thermal requirements, reliability, and commissioning needs—not by TCV alone. A signed compute contract still requires equipment procurement and an operable facility. This supports multiyear demand for integrated infrastructure, but it also means the timing can be disrupted by customer financing or construction delays. Standardization can improve supplier production efficiency while simultaneously increasing customer purchasing power; higher volumes do not automatically imply higher margins.

The near-term trading implication is positive confirmation of the addressable demand environment, not an identifiable Nscale earnings contribution. More decisive catalysts would be named contract awards, manufacturing releases, and shipment schedules. The longer-duration shift favors suppliers capable of integrating power and cooling across complex AI facilities. The inference remains sector-level until specific vendor allocations are disclosed.

CLOUD SERVICES, AI INFRASTRUCTURE, AND PROJECT FINANCE

MICROSOFT GAINS CAPACITY AND PROCUREMENT FLEXIBILITY, WHILE RETAINING SUBSTANTIAL ECONOMIC COMMITMENTS (READ-THROUGH 9)

Microsoft (MSFT: United States) receives a positive, moderate operational read-through, with an important negative qualification for future cost commitments. The S-1 discloses up to $43.8 billion of payments under Microsoft agreements through December 2033, with service terms generally lasting 5–6 years from acceptance of each tranche. It also states that Microsoft expanded its Norway agreement after OpenAI withdrew from the Stargate Norway and UK partnerships. The Norway development is evidence of capacity being reassigned to another large customer, not automatically evidence that the underlying infrastructure demand disappeared. The filing does not state that the UK capacity was similarly replaced. N scale s1 N scale s1

The positive mechanism is access to dedicated infrastructure without Microsoft directly performing every development task. Geographic diversification and an additional delivery channel can support service availability while reducing dependence on any particular internally developed campus. Contractual commencement at acceptance and remedies for breach transfer part of the delivery and performance risk to Nscale. The disclosed expansion of Microsoft’s procurement also provides evidence that a large customer can absorb capacity following a change in another sponsor’s strategy.

The negative mechanism is that outsourcing does not eliminate infrastructure economics. Long-term reserved-capacity commitments can become a cost burden if monetization lags or newer computing alternatives become materially cheaper. Customer advances also require cash before service delivery, although Nscale’s reported 23 percent weighted-average prepayment cannot be assumed to apply specifically to Microsoft. Accounting presentation may differ from direct ownership, but the economic commitment remains real. N scale s1 N scale s1

Near-term catalysts are accepted capacity and evidence that it supports monetizable Azure demand. Contract signing alone is not an Azure revenue event. The longer-duration implication is a broader procurement model combining owned infrastructure with third-party capacity. A critical cross-portfolio safeguard is that Microsoft commitments, Nscale TCV, Dell equipment arrangements, and upstream semiconductor demand are connected parts of the same spending chain and must not be added as independent sources of end demand.

$NSCL NSCALE: SEPTEMBER 2026 S-1 INVESTMENT ANALYSIS (n/1)

EXECUTIVE ASSESSMENT

Nscale represents a substantial AI infrastructure development opportunity, but its economic characteristics differ materially from those of an established hyperscale cloud platform. The company has assembled significant customer commitments, powered-site positions, equipment procurement relationships, and financing capabilities within a short operating history. However, the investment case depends predominantly on converting infrastructure that is not yet operational into accepted customer capacity and, subsequently, into cash returns exceeding the full cost of capital. The appropriate classification is a capital-intensive, contracted development platform with an emerging cloud software business, rather than a mature technology franchise whose principal uncertainty is incremental demand. As of August 2026, Nscale reported $103.4 billion of active and contracted total contract value, or TCV, but only $2.6 billion related to active deployments. Approximately 97.5 percent of disclosed TCV therefore remained associated with capacity outside the active category. N scale s1

The strongest positive evidence is the combination of large customer commitments and improving access to project financing. Microsoft agreements provide for up to $43.8 billion of payments, while Anthropic agreements provide for up to $44.6 billion. Newly established GPU financing facilities for Ward County and North Carolina received investment-grade ratings and carry materially lower contractual spreads than Nscale’s earlier financing arrangements. These developments support the proposition that selected projects can be financed against substantial contractual revenue streams. They do not establish that the entire development program is funded, that all customer contracts possess equivalent credit characteristics, or that the residual equity economics are attractive at an unspecified IPO valuation. N scale s1 N scale s1

The most consequential qualification appears in the financial statement notes. Management’s forecast initially raised substantial doubt about the company’s ability to continue as a going concern because it depended on uncommitted debt and equity financing. Management concluded that the ability to defer, reduce, or cancel capital expenditure would alleviate that doubt. This is not a disclosure of unmitigated going-concern uncertainty, but neither is it evidence that the contracted growth plan is fully financed. It establishes that preserving liquidity under adverse financing conditions may require sacrificing development activity. The fundamental underwriting question is whether Nscale can finance, deliver, and operate its committed portfolio without excessive dilution or project-level economic deterioration. N scale s1

THE OPERATING BASE IS MUCH SMALLER THAN THE DEVELOPMENT PORTFOLIO

The capacity graphic on prospectus page 82 is more informative than the headline power portfolio. It identifies approximately 55 MW of active IT capacity, consisting of 48 MW at colocation facilities and 7 MW at owned facilities. Active and contracted capacity totals approximately 1,370 MW, comprising 1,005 MW at owned sites, 200 MW at leased sites, and 165 MW at colocation sites. Consequently, only approximately 4.0 percent of active and contracted IT capacity was active. Delivering the entire disclosed portfolio would expand operational capacity to approximately 24.9 times the existing active base. This is not a conventional incremental expansion program; it requires a substantial increase in construction, commissioning, operating, and financing throughput. N scale s1

The ownership transition is equally important. Owned facilities represented approximately 12.7 percent of active IT capacity but approximately 73.4 percent of active and contracted capacity. Current operating experience is therefore concentrated in a materially different delivery model from the future portfolio. Colocation deployments demonstrate an ability to install and operate GPU infrastructure, but they provide only partial evidence of the ability to develop large integrated campuses, commission dedicated generation, and manage construction risk directly. Vertical integration can improve coordination and eliminate third-party margins, but it also transfers additional execution obligations onto Nscale’s balance sheet. N scale s1 N scale s1

The facilities table requires careful interpretation. The 5 locations designated as active contain 81 MW of contracted IT capacity in aggregate, whereas the capacity graphic identifies only 55 MW as active. These figures need not be contradictory: a site can be operational while only part of its contracted capacity is revenue generating. Nevertheless, the filing does not provide a detailed site-level reconciliation. Treating the entire contracted capacity of an active site as already delivered would overstate the operating base. Similarly, the defined term “operating data center sites” includes sites under development pursuant to customer contracts; it is not synonymous with energized or revenue-producing facilities. N scale s1 N scale s1

The approximately 10 GW potential power portfolio is another distinct category. Potential capacity depends on future generation development, grid approvals, and related infrastructure. The geographic graphic distinguishes contracted IT load from potential gross power, making a direct comparison between 10 GW of potential power and competitors’ active IT capacity inappropriate. The economically relevant progression is from controlled site rights to permitted power, financed construction, equipment delivery, customer acceptance, and cash-generating operations. Valuation should attach increasing confidence to each completed stage rather than applying a uniform value per announced MW. N scale s1 N scale s1

CUSTOMER QUALITY DOES NOT ELIMINATE CONTRACT PERFORMANCE RISK

Microsoft and Anthropic represent approximately 85.5 percent of aggregate TCV when their disclosed maximum payment amounts are compared with the August 2026 total. This concentration is considerably more important than the number of individual agreements or project subsidiaries. Microsoft agreements span multiple deployments and provide 5–6-year service periods beginning with acceptance of each tranche, with an optional 6-month extension. The disclosed structure offers substantial revenue visibility after delivery, but does not provide an automatic, indefinitely renewable earnings stream. The contract value remains subject to delivery and service availability requirements. N scale s1

The Anthropic agreements introduce a particularly demanding combination of financing and operational requirements. The $44.6 billion arrangement comprises 4 agreements for NVIDIA Vera Rubin deployments at Monarch. Nscale must use best efforts to obtain qualifying financing within a specified period, but had not obtained binding commitments for any financing required to perform those agreements as of the prospectus date. This distinction is critical: a signed customer contract may support a financing process without itself constituting committed financing. The filing does not disclose sufficient detail about the required capital contribution, financing deadline, or prospective lender conditions to demonstrate that the project is financeable on the economics assumed by management. N scale s1

Anthropic’s service requirements are more stringent than those in Nscale’s other customer agreements. Delivery delays receive relief only under specified industry-wide GPU supply constraints and only if binding supplier orders have been placed within a prescribed period. Even qualifying delays can eventually permit termination. Anthropic can terminate a delayed tranche without liability and can terminate for sustained uptime underperformance. These provisions create an important asymmetry: equipment commitments and development spending may precede the point at which customer revenue becomes sufficiently unconditional to support attractive debt financing. The 4 agreements also share a campus, power infrastructure, hardware generation, and customer, limiting their diversification benefit. N scale s1

Take-or-pay protection should therefore be understood narrowly. It reduces exposure to customer utilization decisions once compliant capacity is available, but does not eliminate construction risk, acceptance risk, service-credit exposure, termination rights, or counterparty nonpayment. A highly creditworthy customer can still exercise a valid contractual remedy if Nscale fails to perform. The filing explicitly describes potential penalties, liquidated damages, refunds, and other remedies that could create liquidity pressure independently of access to additional financing. Customer credit quality and provider performance risk require separate underwriting. N scale s1 N scale s1

The Figure partnership broadens the application exposure to physical AI but requires a similar distinction between firm commitments and expansion potential. The S-1 describes potential deployment of up to 100,000 Vera Rubin GPUs beginning in the second half of 2027, alongside a strategic investment in Figure. Separately, Nscale’s September 2026 announcement identifies an initial $3.5 billion compute commitment and an intention to expand beyond $6 billion. The initial commitment, subsequent expansion ambition, and maximum GPU deployment are not interchangeable. The potential 100,000 GPUs should not automatically be added to Nscale’s contracted GPU total, and Nscale’s investment in its customer introduces an additional capital allocation and demand-independence consideration. N scale s1 Nscale

TCV, REMAINING PERFORMANCE OBLIGATIONS, AND CASH ARE DIFFERENT MEASURES

TCV is measured across the full committed term when a customer agreement is signed. It excludes optional extensions, renewals, unexercised capacity, and significant financing components associated with upfront payments. It is therefore neither annual recurring revenue nor remaining cash collections. Dividing $103.4 billion by the 5.7-year weighted-average contract life does not produce a defensible annual revenue forecast because commencement dates, contract durations, delivery tranches, and weighting conventions matter. A project-by-project commissioning schedule is necessary to convert TCV into a revenue forecast. N scale s1 N scale s1

The June 2026 revenue note contains a particularly important accounting adjustment. Remaining performance obligations under ASC 606 totaled $56.4 billion, including $7.1 billion attributable to the significant financing component on customer prepayments. Separately, minimum future customer lease payments under ASC 842 totaled $2.0 billion. Removing the imputed financing component produces approximately $51.3 billion of remaining service and lease revenue on this basis. That remains a revenue-based measure, not an estimate of unpaid customer cash, because remaining revenue can include amounts already prepaid. The $7.1 billion adjustment should not be subtracted from August TCV, which already excludes significant financing components. N scale s1

The financing component matters directly to earnings quality. Customer prepayments are accreted through financing expense, with the corresponding amount ultimately included in revenue as services are delivered. Because adjusted EBITDA excludes interest expense, this mechanism can increase future reported revenue and EBITDA without generating additional contractual cash from the customer. Approximately 12.6 percent of June ASC 606 RPO reflected this financing component. A cash-return model should separate contractual customer payments from imputed financing revenue, while an EBITDA comparison should normalize the associated revenue contribution where material. The filing does not separately disclose enough information to calculate a precise financing-adjusted current EBITDA figure. N scale s1 N scale s1

Accounting classification also should not be mistaken for product differentiation. First-half 2026 revenue comprised $94.7 million of service fees, $42.0 million of lease revenue, and $3.9 million of other revenue. Approximately 67.4 percent was therefore service revenue, but ASC 606 classification does not establish that this revenue possesses software-like margins, retention, or capital intensity. The classification depends on the nature of the arrangement and control of identified assets. A dedicated GPU infrastructure contract can remain economically capital intensive even when accounted for as a service. N scale s1

HISTORICAL LOSSES REQUIRE DISAGGREGATION, NOT DISMISSAL

First-half 2026 revenue increased to $140.6 million from $10.4 million, but cost of revenue excluding depreciation and amortization increased to $189.6 million from $7.8 million. Revenue less this cost category was negative $49.0 million, equivalent to negative 34.9 percent of revenue. This is not a cash gross margin because the expense category includes noncash items, but it demonstrates that the disclosed business had not achieved positive consolidated contribution even before depreciation. Adjusted EBITDA was negative $199.2 million, while adjusted operating loss was $279.6 million. Rapid revenue growth had not yet translated into demonstrated consolidated operating leverage. N scale s1 N scale s1

Lease timing explains part of the disparity between reported losses and current cash costs. Fixed operating lease expense was $155.8 million during the first half, compared with $38.7 million of cash paid against operating lease liabilities. The $117.1 million difference is material and cautions against treating reported rental expense as contemporaneous cash consumption. It does not justify permanently excluding rent from economic analysis. Contractual cash lease payments increase to $268.1 million in 2027 and $314.1 million in 2028, while total undiscounted payments on commenced leases were $5.166 billion. The cost burden changes over time rather than disappearing. N scale s1

The transition toward owned facilities creates another comparability issue. Replacing colocation rent with owned infrastructure can increase EBITDA because costs migrate from operating expense into depreciation, interest, and capital expenditure. That accounting improvement can occur even without a proportionate improvement in economic returns. Ownership creates genuine value when procurement savings, operating efficiencies, residual asset value, and control benefits exceed construction costs, financing costs, and additional risk. Consequently, an expanding EBITDA margin should be evaluated alongside after-maintenance cash flow and returns on total invested capital, rather than interpreted as independent proof of superior economics. The filing itself links anticipated margin expansion partly to replacing leased capacity with owned facilities. N scale s1 N scale s1

Depreciation and amortization also require separation. Of the $174.0 million first-half expense, $77.9 million related to property and equipment and $96.1 million to intangible assets. The majority was therefore intangible amortization, not GPU depreciation. Adjusted operating loss excludes $93.6 million of acquired-intangible amortization but retains most physical-asset depreciation. Both extremes would be misleading: treating all depreciation and amortization as a recurring GPU replacement requirement overstates that requirement, while dismissing physical depreciation entirely ignores substantial capital consumption. Future cash returns depend on hardware replacement economics and customer renewal pricing, not merely the accounting useful life. N scale s1 N scale s1

The $1.020 billion net loss is similarly not equivalent to cash burn. Fair-value losses totaled $457.1 million, including $402.8 million associated with warrant remeasurement and $54.3 million associated with foreign exchange contracts and power swaps. Warrant losses partly reflect an increase in the value of Nscale equity rather than operating deterioration. Nevertheless, warrants represent real transfers of economic value, and market hedges can produce cash settlements. Share-based compensation of $113.8 million, equivalent to approximately 80.9 percent of revenue, is also economically relevant despite being noncash. Excluding these items improves visibility into operations but does not eliminate their significance to common shareholders. N scale s1 N scale s1

POSITIVE OPERATING CASH FLOW IS PREDOMINANTLY A FUNDING PHENOMENON

Reported first-half operating cash flow of $1.686 billion should not be interpreted as evidence that the operating platform is self-funding. The cash flow statement includes a $3.812 billion benefit from deferred revenue and a $1.505 billion use associated with accounts receivable. Those categories contributed a net $2.306 billion. Mechanically excluding both leaves negative $620.0 million of operating cash flow. This adjustment is not a forecast of normalized cash burn, since other working-capital movements and development-stage costs remain, but it shows that positive reported operating cash flow depended on the contractual funding cycle rather than positive underlying earnings. N scale s1

Customer prepayments are a legitimate and potentially valuable financing advantage. They reduce the amount of capital that must be supplied by debt and equity investors and can improve project returns substantially. However, they are advance consideration for future services, not incremental profit. The reported weighted-average prepayment was 23 percent of active and contracted TCV. That percentage cannot be applied to the entire TCV balance and then added to existing liquidity without accounting for amounts already received, amounts merely billed, funds already spent or pledged, and future services still owed. As deployment growth moderates, prepaid revenue will continue to be recognized while associated operating costs require cash, reducing the benefit from new advances. N scale s1

The deferred revenue roll-forward makes the cash distinction explicit. The balance increased from $2.039 billion to $6.493 billion, incorporating $4.376 billion billed in advance, $120.3 million of financing accretion, and $42.4 million of recognized revenue. Accounts receivable reached $1.928 billion. Deferred revenue therefore should not be equated with cash already collected, and conventional revenue-based receivables ratios would be difficult to interpret where invoices include large advance payments. Cash expenditure on property and equipment was $3.230 billion, leaving operating cash flow less those purchases at negative $1.544 billion, or negative $1.560 billion including purchased intangible assets. N scale s1 N scale s1 N scale s1

CAPITAL REQUIREMENTS EXCEED WHAT HEADLINE CASH OR DEBT BALANCES REVEAL

At June 2026, unrestricted cash and equivalents totaled $1.478 billion, while an additional $614.7 million was restricted. The company also reported $317.3 million of VAT receivables and $1.411 billion of accounts payable and accrued expenses. These balances have different liquidity characteristics. Restricted cash cannot be treated as freely available expansion capital, VAT recovery depends on timing and administrative processes, and supplier liabilities represent future cash requirements rather than permanent financing. The balance sheet also included approximately $430.7 million of outstanding consideration for the SIN02 acquisition. N scale s1 N scale s1 N scale s1 N scale s1

Outstanding commitments included $24.0 billion for undelivered technology equipment and $3.5 billion for data center construction and supporting services, payable primarily during 2026 and 2027. Another $1.4 billion of undiscounted obligations related to leases that had not commenced. These figures are not equivalent to an immediate $28.9 billion cash deficit: payment schedules, customer advances, financing availability, cancellation rights, and subsequent events matter. Equally, they cannot be dismissed because reported debt was small. The June commitments also precede the August Anthropic agreements and therefore do not define the full capital requirement associated with the latest contracted portfolio. N scale s1 N scale s1

The going-concern mitigation depends on capital expenditure flexibility, but the commercial cost of exercising that flexibility is not fully quantified. Deferring a speculative project can preserve cash with limited near-term damage. Deferring equipment for a committed deployment can trigger lost revenue, customer termination, penalties, or financing consequences. The essential liquidity analysis is therefore a monthly, tranche-level comparison of unavoidable supplier payments, cancellable commitments, customer advance receipts, financing conditions, acceptance dates, and potential remedies. The filing supports management’s conclusion that expenditure can be reduced sufficiently to preserve liquidity; it does not demonstrate that such reductions would preserve the entire TCV or the contemplated equity valuation. N scale s1 N scale s1
